title: Generics & launch 1: Generic drug basics
disclaimer: An educational course for project management of generic launches. It is not regulatory, legal or quality advice: EU rules are the anchor, and national and company practice vary.

blocks.markdown:
## Every generic has a reference

A generic application doesn't prove safety and efficacy from scratch. Instead it relies on a **reference medicinal product** (*médicament de référence*): a medicine authorised in the EU on the basis of a complete dossier of its own, with quality, non-clinical and clinical data. Choosing and documenting the right reference product is one of the first things regulatory affairs settles.

blocks.caption: Reference product vs generic: what must match

blocks.alt: Pharmacy shelf: Bayer Aspirin 500 mg boxes priced 11.99 beside store-brand acetylsalicylic acid 500 mg boxes priced 8.99
blocks.caption: Branded original and store-brand generic side by side (Canada)

blocks.markdown:
## What 'generic' means in EU law

Under Art. 10(2)(b), a generic has three things in common with its reference product:

- the same qualitative and quantitative composition in active substances
- the same pharmaceutical form
- **bioequivalence** (*bioéquivalence*), shown by appropriate studies (Lesson 2)

Different salts, esters or isomers of the same substance count as the same active substance, unless they differ significantly in safety or efficacy. All immediate-release oral forms, such as tablets and capsules, count as one pharmaceutical form.

## A reference from another EU country

The reference product doesn't have to be authorised in the country where the generic is filed. Under the **European reference product** (*médicament de référence européen*) rule in Art. 10(1), it can be a product authorised in another EU member state. The application then names that state, and its authority confirms the reference's details.

## The global marketing authorisation

All the strengths, forms and presentations the originator adds later belong to one **global marketing authorisation** (*autorisation globale de mise sur le marché*). This is set out in Art. 6(1). The protection clock therefore starts once, with the very first authorisation. A new strength launched years later doesn't restart it.

**What this means for the launch timeline:** the reference product determines when you may file and launch (Lesson 4), and the reference batches the bioequivalence study must use. A wrong or unavailable reference product can stall the whole project.

All later strengths and forms of the originator count as one authorisation, so the protection clock starts once. FR: autorisation globale de mise sur le marché.

questions.stem: The originator launched a new 5 mg strength six years after its first EU approval. When does its data protection period start?
options: From the first EU authorisation of the product, under the global marketing authorisation
questions.explanation: Under Art. 6(1), later strengths belong to the same global marketing authorisation, so the clock runs from the first authorisation.

## What bioequivalence proves

If the generic releases the active substance into the blood at the same rate and to the same extent as the reference, it's expected to work the same way. A bioequivalence study measures exactly that. Usually healthy volunteers take each product in turn, in a **crossover design** (*plan croisé*), and blood samples are taken over time.

blocks.alt: Blood-level curves over time for reference and generic, nearly overlapping, with peak (Cmax) and area under the curve marked, and an 80–125% acceptance band
blocks.caption: Bioequivalence in one picture

blocks.markdown:
## Two numbers that matter

- **Cmax**: the peak blood level, which reflects how fast the substance gets in
- **AUC** (area under the curve): the total exposure, meaning how much gets in overall

Both numbers are compared between the generic and the reference, as a ratio.

## The usual EU test

Under the EMA bioequivalence guideline, the 90% **confidence interval** (*intervalle de confiance*) of the generic/reference ratio must lie within 80.00–125.00%, for both AUC and Cmax. Two exceptions apply:

- For narrow-therapeutic-index substances, where small changes matter clinically, the range can be tightened to 90.00–111.11%.
- For highly variable substances, the Cmax range can, under conditions, be widened, up to 69.84–143.19%.

'80–125%' doesn't mean a generic may deliver 20% less drug. The averages are usually close to 100%. What must fit inside the range is the uncertainty around that average.

## When a study fails

If the confidence interval falls outside the range, the product can't be shown to be bioequivalent. Typical responses are reformulating the product, or running a larger study. In both cases this means months of delay, and often a new batch.

**What this means for the launch timeline:** the bioequivalence study is usually the longest scientific step before submission in own development. For in-licensed dossiers, check early that the study used an EU reference product, and that its report is complete.

cards.back: Same rate and extent of absorption as the reference. Tested with the 90% CI of the AUC and Cmax ratios, which must fall within 80–125%. FR: bioéquivalence.
Cmax: peak blood level (speed). AUC: total exposure (amount).

questions.stem: What does the 80–125% rule actually require?
options: The generic contains 80–125% of the stated dose
The 90% confidence interval of the generic/reference ratio for AUC and Cmax lies within 80–125%
questions.explanation: It applies to the confidence interval of the ratio. In practice, passing products have average ratios close to 100%.

## Not every strength needs its own study

A **biowaiver** (*dispense d'étude de bioéquivalence*) is permission not to run an in-vivo bioequivalence study for a particular strength or product. Instead, the applicant shows in the lab why one isn't needed.

blocks.alt: One bioequivalence study at the highest strength covering three lower strengths, provided five conditions are met
blocks.caption: One study, several strengths

blocks.markdown:
## Additional-strength biowaiver

Under the EMA guideline, a study on one strength can cover the others if five conditions are all met:

1. The same manufacturing process.
2. The same qualitative composition.
3. Proportional composition.
4. Similar dissolution profiles in the lab.
5. Pharmacokinetics that behave linearly over the dose range.

Which strength must be studied depends on the substance.

## BCS-based biowaiver

For some substances, a whole study can be replaced by lab data under the **Biopharmaceutics Classification System** (BCS), set out in the ICH M9 guideline. This is possible mainly for highly soluble substances in immediate-release forms that meet strict criteria. It's less common, but very valuable when it applies.

## Dissolution testing

Both kinds of waiver rely on **dissolution testing** (*essai de dissolution*): measuring how fast the tablet releases the substance in the lab, usually at several pH levels. The waiver stands or falls on those comparisons.

**What this means for the launch timeline:** biowaivers save months and money. When a range of strengths is planned, ask early which strength has the bioequivalence study and whether the waiver conditions are documented.

cards.back: Permission to skip an in-vivo BE study, based on lab data (additional-strength or BCS-based). FR: dispense d'étude de bioéquivalence.
Biopharmaceutics Classification System. It can justify replacing a BE study for some highly soluble, immediate-release substances (ICH M9).

options: Nothing; each needs its own study
An additional-strength biowaiver, if the process, composition, proportionality, dissolution and linear pharmacokinetics conditions are met
questions.explanation: The EMA guideline sets the conditions under which one study can support the other strengths.

## Two separate clocks

A new medicine gets regulatory protection that has nothing to do with patents. There are two periods:

- **Data protection** (*protection des données*): generics can't refer to the originator's data, so they can't even file.
- **Market protection** (*protection commerciale*): generics may file and be approved, but they can't be placed on the market yet.

Patents and supplementary protection certificates (SPCs) run in parallel and are covered in Module 3.

blocks.alt: Two timelines: current rules with 8 years of data protection, 2 years of market protection and an optional extra year; reform with 8 years plus 1 year plus extensions, capped at 11 years
blocks.caption: When can a generic file, and when can it launch?

blocks.markdown:
## Today's rule: 8 + 2 (+1)

Under Art. 10(1) of Directive 2001/83/EC:

- A generic may be **filed** 8 years after the reference product's first EU authorisation.
- It may be **placed on the market** after 10 years.
- The 10 years become 11 if, during the first 8 years, the originator obtained a new indication bringing a significant clinical benefit.

## The reform: 8 + 1, with extensions

In December 2025, the Parliament and the Council reached political agreement on the EU 'pharma package', which will replace Directive 2001/83/EC. It keeps 8 years of data protection but cuts the standard market protection to **1 year**. Extensions are possible, for example for a significant new indication, up to a combined cap of 11 years. The package also widens the Bolar exemption (Module 3).

The new rules apply only after formal adoption and a transition period. The EMA expects them to become applicable around 2028. Under the agreed transitional rules, reference products whose marketing authorisation application was submitted before the new law enters into force keep today's protection periods. So for practically every reference product you'll meet in the coming years, today's 8 + 2 (+1) applies.

## How a PM uses this

For each product and country, keep three dates:

1. the earliest filing date (data protection end)
2. the earliest regulatory launch date (market protection end)
3. the earliest legal launch date once patents and SPCs are included (Module 3)

The launch date is the latest of these.
**What this means for the launch timeline:** filing can, and should, start before launch is allowed. Many teams file around year 8 so that approval lands just as market protection ends.

cards.back: Period during which generics can't refer to the originator's data, so they can't file. Today 8 years. FR: protection des données.
Period during which generics may be approved but not sold. Today 2 years (+1 for a significant new indication); reform: 1 year plus extensions, capped at 11. FR: protection commerciale.
File from year 8, launch from year 10 (or 11), counted from the reference product's first EU authorisation.

questions.stem: A reference product was first authorised in the EU in March 2018, with no new indication. Under today's rules, when may a generic be placed on the market (ignoring patents)?
questions.explanation: 8 years of data protection plus 2 years of market protection gives 10 years from March 2018, so March 2028. Filing was possible from March 2026.

questions.stem: What does the 2025–2026 pharma package change for standard market protection?
options: It cuts it from 2 years to 1 year, with possible extensions up to a combined cap of 11 years
questions.explanation: Data protection stays at 8 years. Market protection becomes 1 year plus possible extensions. The rules apply only after adoption and transition.

## Every application has a legal basis

The **legal basis** (*base légale*) is the article of Directive 2001/83/EC an application is filed under. It decides which data the dossier must contain and which data it may borrow, and it's one of the first decisions in any project.

blocks.alt: Decision tree: EU reference plus bioequivalence leads to Art. 10(1), else 10(3) hybrid; no reference and known substances combined leads to 10b; otherwise 10a or 8(3); 10c shown apart
blocks.caption: Choosing the legal basis: a simplified tree

blocks.markdown:
## The six routes in one line each

- **Art. 10(1), generic:** relies on the reference product's data and adds quality data and bioequivalence (Lessons 1–2).
- **Art. 10(3), hybrid:** (*demande hybride*) used when the product isn't strictly a generic, for example a different strength, form, route or indication, or when bioequivalence alone isn't enough. It relies on the reference product plus bridging studies.
- **Art. 10a, well-established use:** (*usage médical bien établi*) the substance has been in well-established medical use in the EU for at least 10 years, so published literature replaces the company's own studies.
- **Art. 10b, fixed combination:** known substances combined in a new way (Lesson 6).
- **Art. 10c, informed consent:** (*consentement éclairé*) another MAH allows its full dossier to be used for an identical product.
- **Art. 8(3), full or mixed:** the company's own complete dossier (Lesson 7).

### Process card: Choosing the legal basis

- What it is: the decision on which article of Directive 2001/83/EC the application uses
- Who owns it: Regulatory affairs, with input from the dossier owner and, if needed, scientific advice from an authority
- Inputs: reference product availability, bioequivalence data, product differences, protection dates
- Output: a documented legal basis and a list of the data required
- Typical duration: days for a clear generic; weeks to months if a hybrid or a combination needs advice
- What makes it slip: reference product unavailable in the EU, failed or missing bioequivalence, unclear protection dates
- PM watch-points: get this decision in writing before the timeline is fixed, because it determines what has to be produced

**What this means for the launch timeline:** the legal basis sets the length of the work before filing. A switch late in the project, for example from generic to hybrid, often means new studies and months of delay.

cards.back: The article of Directive 2001/83/EC an application is filed under. It decides which data are needed. FR: base légale.
Used when the product differs from the reference (strength, form, route, indication) or bioequivalence isn't enough. Reference data plus bridging studies. FR: demande hybride.
Another MAH allows its full dossier to be used for an identical product. FR: consentement éclairé.

questions.stem: A company wants to launch an oral solution, but the reference product exists only as tablets. Which basis is most likely?
questions.explanation: A different pharmaceutical form falls outside the generic definition, so the hybrid route, with bridging data, is the usual option.

## Known pieces, new combination

Art. 10b covers a medicine that combines active substances already used in authorised medicines, but not yet authorised together in that combination. The single substances are well known. What's new is putting them in one product.

blocks.alt: Substances A and B joined in one tablet, with the data needed: full quality data, new studies on the combination, often bioequivalence vs the separate products; single substances not re-proved
blocks.caption: Art. 10b: two known substances, one new product

blocks.markdown:
## What the dossier must show

Under Art. 10b, the application must give the results of new non-clinical or clinical studies on the **combination**. It doesn't have to provide scientific references for each substance on its own. Full quality data for the new product are always required.

In practice, the EMA guideline on **fixed combination medicinal products** (*associations fixes*) explains what's expected. A common element is a bioequivalence study comparing the combined tablet with the substances taken as separate products. That shows the combination behaves like the free combination doctors already use.

## 10b or a generic of a combination?

If an authorised A+B product already exists and its protection has expired, a new A+B product may be filed as a **generic of that combination** under Art. 10(1), which is usually simpler. Art. 10b is the route when no authorised A+B reference exists, or when the product can't rely on it.

## Why companies choose 10b

Companies use fixed combinations to make treatment simpler: one tablet instead of two. They're common in cardiometabolic medicines, for example combining two cholesterol medicines. The Medicines modules in this app list several, such as rosuvastatin with ezetimibe, or bempedoic acid with ezetimibe.

**What this means for the launch timeline:** 10b projects usually need new studies, often a bioequivalence study of the combination against the separate products. Plan the study, its reference batches of both single products, and the time to report it before filing.

cards.back: Known substances newly combined in one product. New data on the combination are required; data on each single substance aren't. FR: association fixe (art. 10b).
If an authorised A+B product exists and its protection has expired, an A+B generic under Art. 10(1) may be possible. Otherwise, 10b.

questions.stem: Which statement about an Art. 10b application is correct?

It can only be used for biologicals
It needs the other MAH's consent
questions.explanation: Art. 10b requires data on the combination. Each known substance doesn't need to be re-proved on its own.

## When you can't borrow

Art. 8(3) is the standard route for a new medicine: a complete dossier with the company's own quality, non-clinical and clinical data. In the generics world it's less common, but you'll meet it. For example, when there's no usable EU reference product, or when a product is filed on a dossier written to stand on its own.

blocks.alt: Three dossier stacks: Art. 8(3) full with own non-clinical and clinical data; 8(3) mixed with own studies plus literature; 10(1) generic relying on the reference plus a bioequivalence study
blocks.caption: What's inside the dossier, by legal basis

blocks.markdown:
## Full vs mixed

A **full application** (*demande complète*) contains the company's own studies in every module.

A **mixed application** (*demande mixte*) is still filed under Art. 8(3), but combines the company's own studies with published scientific literature for parts of the non-clinical or clinical documentation. Annex I of the Directive describes it.

## Quality is never borrowed

Whatever the legal basis, the quality part of the dossier (CTD Module 3) always describes your own product: its substance, manufacture, controls and stability. For a PM, this matters: quality documentation comes from the manufacturer on every route, and gaps in it delay every route equally.

## Why it matters for planning

Full and mixed dossiers carry the most pre-submission work and the most assessment questions. When an in-licensed dossier is labelled '8(3)', check what it really contains (own studies or literature) during the gap analysis in Module 2.
**What this means for the launch timeline:** an Art. 8(3) dossier means the longest preparation and usually more assessment questions. Budget extra clock-stop time for responses.

cards.back: Filed under Art. 8(3), combining own studies with published literature (Directive 2001/83/EC, Annex I). FR: demande mixte.
CTD Module 3 always describes your own product, on every legal basis. It's never borrowed.

questions.stem: Which part of the dossier is always the applicant's own, whatever the legal basis?

## Three questions to ask on any new project

1. What's the legal basis, and is it confirmed in writing?
2. What's the reference product, when was it first authorised in the EU, and so when can we file and launch?
3. Which studies exist (bioequivalence, combination, bridging), and which still have to be done?

The answers give the first draft of the pre-submission timeline.

questions.stem: A project combines two known substances, and no A+B product exists in the EU. Which basis is likely, and what's the main extra work?
options: 10b; new studies on the combination, often bioequivalence against the separate products
questions.explanation: Without an existing A+B reference product, Art. 10b applies, and the combination needs its own data.

questions.stem: A reference product was first authorised in the EU in June 2017. Under today's rules, when may a generic be filed, ignoring patents?
questions.explanation: Eight years of data protection runs to June 2025. Launch is possible from June 2027, or 2028 if a significant new indication was granted.

questions.stem: Why does a late switch from generic to hybrid hurt the timeline?
options: A hybrid needs bridging data, which usually means new studies and months of work before filing
Hybrids need consent from the originator
questions.explanation: The legal basis decides what data are needed. Changing it late adds studies to the critical path.
